source.title: Federal Bureau of Investigation Internet Crime Report 2025
source.covers: Complaints filed at ic3.gov in calendar year 2025
source.license: Work of the United States Government; not subject to copyright in the United States.

how_extracted: Table cells were read from the PDF text layer by position, then checked against the page images. Ten cells that the PDF wraps or overprints (p.33, p.37, p.50) were read from the page by hand. Charts without a data table (pp.4, 9, 10, 13, 16, 18, 24, 34, 52) were transcribed from their printed labels. Every section carries the page it came from.
caveats: These are complaints people chose to file with the FBI, so they are a floor. Most scams are never reported.
Each complaint has one crime type. Descriptors (Cryptocurrency, AI Related, Crimes Against Children) are tags added on top of a crime type, so they overlap with the crime types and with each other.
The 26 crime types add up to 768,452 complaints and $20.30 billion, less than the 1,008,597 complaints and $20.877 billion in the headline. The report does not explain the difference.
Complainants are not required to give an age. Complaints without one are left out of every age table.
State figures count complaints that gave a state, not people. One person can file more than once.
Loss figures are what complainants reported, adjusted by IC3 analysts. They can change after publication.
Ransomware losses leave out lost business, time, wages, files, equipment and outside remediation, and organisations often report no loss at all.
Rates per 100,000 use the 2025 Census population estimates and cover the 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico.

discrepancies.detail: 21,333 complaints and $1,040,730,043 on pp.45-46; 21,334 and $1,040,879,243 in the three-year table on pp.47-48. Both are kept: by_age.60_plus uses pp.45-46, sixty_plus_by_year uses pp.47-48.
349 complaints and $394,040 on pp.45-46; 348 and $244,840 on pp.47-48. Both are kept, as above.
42,271 complaints and $4,347,081,557 in the Elder Fraud section (pp.45-46); 44,555 and $4,432,224,488 in the Cryptocurrency section (p.52).
The age tables use 'Under 20'; the minors section uses '17 years old or younger'. They are different groups and are stored separately.

discrepancies.what: Elder fraud loss in the accessibility text
discrepancies.detail: Footnote 17 on p.44 prints '$7,748 billion'; the figure is $7.748 billion ($7,748,911,371 on p.6).

headline.complaints_per_day_note: The report says IC3 now averages almost 3,000 complaints a day (p.3); 1,008,597 / 365 = 2,763.

history.note: Only the points labelled on the two charts. The year for two labelled points (303,809 and 288,012 complaints) cannot be read off the chart with certainty and they are left out.

cyber_enabled_fraud.payment_methods_note: Top reported ways victims paid, as a share of each crime type's reported transactions (p.10 pie charts). Only the slices printed with a label are listed, so rows do not add to 100.

rows.label: Call center fraud (tech support and government impersonation)

investment_fraud.forced_labour_link: These scams are largely perpetrated by organized criminal enterprises based in Southeast Asia using victims of human trafficking as forced labor to run the scam operations. (p.11)

recovery_scams.note: Losses may include what was lost to the earlier scam that led the person to the 'recovery' firm.

ai.note: Counted only when the complaint mentions AI. The report says many victims do not realise AI was involved.

recovery_asset_team.note: IC3's Recovery Asset Team asks banks to freeze fraudulent transfers (the Financial Fraud Kill Chain). Speed matters: tell your bank at once, then file at ic3.gov with the full transaction details.

operation_level_up.note: FBI operation, launched January 2024, that finds people in the middle of a cryptocurrency investment scam and tells them.
